My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Rajesh is a 32-year-old South Asian man who has been working as a housekeeper for several years. He is married and his life was relatively stable until he experienced a traumatic event—a mugging—that has profoundly altered how he perceives the world around him. One chilly evening, Rajesh was walking home from work when he was suddenly confronted by two men demanding his wallet. In the struggle that ensued, one of the assailants hit him on the head with a blunt object, causing severe pain and injury. The memory of this event is exceptionally vivid; every detail comes back to him in sharp relief, including the cold metal of the object hitting his skull and the fear he felt as he realized his life was in danger. Since that night, Rajesh has found it almost impossible to talk about what happened without feeling overwhelmed by physical pain. The memory resurfaces often, triggered by anything reminiscent of the event—dark alleys on his way home from work or a sudden loud noise in an otherwise quiet room. When these memories return, he feels the same intense physical discomfort as if the trauma were happening all over again. Rajesh’s traumatic experience has also deeply affected his trust in others. He now believes that people are not what they seem and can’t be trusted. This mistrust is pervasive; it colors every interaction he has, making him wary of even the most benign encounters. As a housekeeper, Rajesh frequently finds himself in situations where he must engage with new clients or interact with strangers in public spaces. Each encounter feels like walking on eggshells because he’s certain that danger lurks behind every smile. The vividness and painful recollections of the mugging have only reinforced his negative appraisals. Every time a memory resurfaces, Rajesh is reminded of how unsafe the world can be, solidifying his belief that people are inherently untrustworthy. This cycle has left him feeling isolated and on edge, constantly scanning for signs of potential threats. Rajesh’s sense of distrust and danger exacerbates his memory disturbances. When he experiences vivid flashbacks or intrusive thoughts, it fuels his negative beliefs about the world, making him even more guarded and suspicious. He often wakes up in a cold sweat, replaying the event over and over again, each time reinforcing his belief that the world is dangerous. These ongoing fears have begun to affect his work. Rajesh has started skipping certain shifts or avoiding parts of his job that require walking alone at night, leading to conflicts with his employers. His marriage has also been strained; he keeps to himself more often and avoids social situations, which has left his wife feeling concerned about his wellbeing. Despite these challenges, Rajesh’s deteriorating mental state finally prompted him to seek help. He is most afraid of never being able to feel safe again and living with constant vigilance. At the same time, he hopes that therapy might provide a way to manage his memories and regain some trust in others and in life itself. In summary, Rajesh’s experience has left him with vivid, painful memories of the mugging, which fuel his deeply ingrained beliefs about the world being dangerous and untrustworthy. This cycle of negative appraisals and intrusive memories has significantly impacted his daily functioning and relationships, leading to a decision to seek psychological help in order to regain some semblance of normalcy and safety in his life.
